text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co on Thursday unveiled a range of new products aimed at helping customers get their businesses established on the Internet and to develop intranet internal networks using the technology.
The comprehensive set of offerings includes professional consulting and support programs and resale channel activities while providing a choice of both Unix and Windows NT systems.
The new offerings also include five Unix-based HP Domain Enterprise Servers combining hardware and software for up to 1,360 users ranging in U.S. list price from $9,500 to $85,000.

Palo Alto-based HP said its HP NetServer Web Master, with a U.S. list price of $9,999, was the industry's first integrated Internet personal computer-based server package based on Microsoft Corp's Windows NT platform.
"We believe that people will need both Unix and NT," Dick Watts, vice president and general manager of HP's Computer Systems Organization, said in an interview.
"What we've done here is establish the platform -- hardware, software and services -- to enable a lot of applications, publishing, authoring, e-commerce, collaboration and electronic mail."

Watts contrasted Hewlett-Packard's combination of Unix and NT to rivals Sun Microsystems Inc, which has built new business around its work on the Java platform used for Internet software but has turned up its nose at the prospect of supplying machines with NT, and Compaq Computer Corp, which supplies servers for NT without a Unix base.
"I don't see it as one or the other. We're riding one horse that is both Unix and NT," he said, adding he had not found any customers who did not expect to deploy both systems.

Each of the company's HP Domain Servers is bundled with HP Domain Business Suite software, Netscale SuiteSpot or Netscape Enterprise Server software, a 100-user HP OpenMail license, the HP Domain Server Management System, a Java Developer's Kit and the Java Virtual Machine.

The servers range from a 100 megahertz unit with a PA7100LC reduced instruction set (RISC) processor, 32 magabytes of random access memory (RAM), a quad-speed CD-ROM and two gigabytes of storage to a 180-megahertz PA8000-based server with 128 megabytes of RAM and four gigabytes of storage.

HP said it was also introducing a partnering program to help develop Internet and intranet solutions across NT and Unix environments and that it was "arming" its channel partners to provide know-how and tools for expanded offerings.
